one_liner: Rust and hand-written assembly WebP decoder with a C ABI; 1.04-1.76x faster than libwebp 1.6.0 on one thread.
what_it_does: wpd decodes WebP stills (lossy VP8, lossless VP8L, alpha) and animations (composited canvas or raw sub-frames) into planar YUV420P/YUVA420P or packed RGB(A), BGR(A), ARGB, premultiplied, RGB565 and RGBA4444 output, with crop, scale, flip, streaming (open_stream/append/partial_frame) and a frame_size_limit for hostile input. It ships a C ABI (include/wpd.h: wpd_decoder_create/open/next_frame plus one-shot wpd_decode and wpd_decode_into), installed by Meson as static and shared libraries with wpd.pc, and a Rust API (Decoder::open, next_frame, rows_of). It is not source-compatible with libwebp's WebPDecode/WebPAnimDecoder calls, but its parity tests compare output bytes with libwebp's for every packed format.
how_it_is_fast: The DSP kernels (VP8 IDCT, loop filters and intra predictors, VP8L predictors, colour transforms and palette mapping, alpha unfiltering, premultiply/blend, YUV-to-RGB with fancy upsampling) are hand-written NASM for x86 (C, SSE2, SSSE3, SSE4.1 and AVX2 variants chosen at run time) and assembly for AArch64 and 32-bit ARM, each checked against the reference by checkasm. AVX2_BENCHMARKS.md profiles about 74% of lossless cycles in VP8L entropy decoding (decode_pixels) and about 49% of lossy cycles in coefficient decoding, so most of the lossless and animation gain comes from the Rust entropy, compositing and output paths rather than SIMD. For YUV420P output wpd hands out its own decoded planes instead of copying them into a separate buffer. An optional thread pool (n_threads) runs parallel pipelines and decodes animation frames ahead; the published table uses one thread.
when_to_use: Decode-heavy services or apps whose WebP traffic is mostly lossless stills or animations: 1.76x on lossless.webp (576x576, to RGBA), 1.67x on anim_rgb.webp (12 frames, 400x400) and 1.32x on anim_yuva.webp versus single-threaded libwebp.
Pipelines that want planar YUV420 or YUVA420 (video encoders, GPU texture upload), since wpd returns its internal planes without a copy.

Decoding untrusted WebP where libwebp's C history (CVE-2023-4863) is a concern: Rust core, a fuzz target, frame_size_limit to cap memory before allocation, and an -Denable_asm=false build for full memory-safety guarantees at a speed cost.
C or C++ projects on x86-64 or AArch64 that can add Cargo, Meson and nasm to the build and link a static or shared library through wpd.h.
when_not_to_use: Mostly lossy photos: the gain is 1.04x and 1.08x to YUV420P and 1.03x to 1.05x to RGBA, close to libwebp's speed.
Palette (colour-indexed) lossless images: the whole-corpus run in AVX2_BENCHMARKS.md (commit 0a453d8) had wpd slower than libwebp on palette2bpp_rgb.webp (0.629x) and palette_rgb.webp (0.775x).
You need encoding, or a crates.io release, a CMake or Bazel build, or a toolchain without Rust: wpd is decoder-only, version 0.2.0, consumed as a git dependency or through Meson.

You need settled, audited code: the project is months old with fast churn (the AVX2 kernels landed 2026-10-01, the day after the table was measured), and a September 2026 audit fixed an out-of-bounds write in the AArch64 loop-filter assembly and an out-of-bounds read in the ARM32 one (PR #30).
Large images: the published workload tops out at 1024x1024, so behaviour on multi-megapixel photos is not measured.

integration.form: static lib + shared lib (C ABI, wpd.pc); Rust crate via git dependency
integration.dependencies: Build: Rust toolchain with Cargo, Meson >= 1.4.0, nasm on x86 (crate build uses cc and nasm-rs); crate dependency zerocopy 0.8; runtime libm and pthreads
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.82 (rust-version), C11 for the C parts, Meson 1.4.0; -Dnightly_size needs nightly Rust with rust-src
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 with NASM (ELF64, Win64 and Mach-O64 assemble; runtime checks ran on Linux only), AArch64 and 32-bit ARM assembly, portable Rust paths with -Denable_asm=false; Linux, macOS and Windows targets in the build files
integration.thread_safety: One call at a time per decoder handle, including const queries (external synchronization); different handles can be used concurrently. With n_threads other than 1 the decoder starts worker threads and the process-global log callback may be called concurrently from them.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — different API (wpd_decoder_* / wpd_decode instead of WebPDecode and WebPAnimDecoder), but parity tests require byte-identical output to libwebp, so switching is a call-site rewrite rather than a behaviour change

gotchas: n_threads = 0, the default in both the Rust Options and the CLI, means every processor the process may use; set 1 to get libwebp-like single-threaded behaviour (a C decoder stays on one thread only until options are set).

Decoder-owned frame memory, including the zero-copy YUV planes, is invalidated by the next call on that decoder; use wpd_decoder_set_output_buffer or wpd_decode_into for caller-owned memory. wpd_decoder_open copies the input; open_borrowed does not.

Assembly is on by default, so the memory-safety claim holds fully only with -Denable_asm=false; the -Dnightly_size sealed library aborts the process on an internal panic instead of returning WPD_ERR_INTERNAL.

Older README tables and the 'Introducing wpd' blog post (seen as a search snippet only: 1.61x-2.92x versus libwebp, 2.17x-4.56x versus image-webp) predate commit 0a453d8, which made both decoders emit the same pixel format; quote only the current table.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No other WebP decoder is catalogued: the pure-Rust image-webp 0.2.4, timed in the same harness, is slower than libwebp on every RGBA row (lossless 231.50 versus 195.75 ms, anim_yuva 776.54 versus 494.37 ms), so wpd is the pick when you want a Rust-based decoder that beats libwebp rather than trails it; @napi-rs/image is a Node.js binding over libwebp, not an alternative decoder.
verified_claims_summary: First-party: scripts/bench.sh runs hyperfine -N (3 warmups, 20 runs) on one process doing 48 decodes, on an Intel Core i7-13700K pinned to CPU 0, comparing wpd --threads 1 with tools/libwebpdec.c over a static libwebp 1.6.0 (pinned 94d3c4a, built through Meson's CMake subproject, use_threads off), both producing the same output format; medians were 173.56 versus 180.40 ms for a 1024x1024 lossy still to YUV420P (1.04x), 111.27 versus 195.75 ms for a 576x576 lossless still to RGBA (1.76x) and 62.56 versus 104.47 ms for a 400x400 12-frame animation (1.67x); rustc, C compiler and nasm versions are not stated. Reading both drivers: each iteration builds a fresh decoder, wpd still runs the requested conversion when output goes to /dev/null, wpd also copies the input on every open, and the YUV rows compare libwebp writing into a separately allocated output buffer with wpd handing out its own planes; I found no correctness bug behind the numbers.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-10-03, 34 pull requests, 12 stars, version 0.2.0, not on crates.io) and BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE file added 2026-10-03), so copyable, but young enough that you should pin a commit and run its parity, checkasm and testdata suites before shipping.
